dataset.what_one_row_represents: One film with its IMDb 'movie connections' count, plus its Oscars Best Picture status (winner, nominee, or neither). Limited to top-100 films per release year.
dataset.geographic_scope: Global cinema, but heavily Western/Hollywood weighted via IMDb users

ana_01.label: Dataset profile
ana_01.content: After capping at 2016 releases (the Economist's own boundary), the dataset has 28,763 film-rows spanning 1926-2016. Of these, 89 films are tagged W (Best Picture winner), 442 are tagged N (Best Picture nominee), and 28,232 are unrecognized by Best Picture. Every row carries a year_rank (1-100 within its release year) and an annual_share (count / total references for that year).

ana_02.label: Top 20 most-referenced films of all time
ana_02.content: Star Wars (1977) tops the all-time list with 4,965 IMDb connections, capturing 55.2% of all references for films released in 1977. The Wizard of Oz (1939) is second with 3,291 references (50.3% of 1939). The Godfather (1972) is third with 1,767 (33.7%) and is the highest-ranked Best Picture winner on the all-time list. Of the all-time top 20, only 4 are Best Picture winners: The Godfather, Casablanca, Gone with the Wind, and Titanic. Ten films in the top 20 were never even nominated, including Empire Strikes Back, Psycho, The Terminator, and 2001: A Space Odyssey.

ana_03.label: Year-rank distribution of Best Picture winners
ana_03.content: Across 89 Best Picture winners, the median year_rank is 7 and the mean is 8.0. Only 14 of 89 winners (15.7%) were the most-referenced film of their year. A quarter of winners ranked 10th or worse. The worst case is Cavalcade (1933), ranked 37th in its year. The Last Emperor (1987) ranked 36th. This distribution shows that the Academy's choice frequently does not match the year's most-influential film, even by the Academy's own time horizon.

ana_04.label: Best Picture winners' year-rank, by decade
ana_04.content: The mean year_rank of Best Picture winners shows the Academy was sharpest in the 1970s (mean 3.5, with 30% ranked #1) and weakest in the 1980s (mean 14.0, no rank-1 winners). The 2010s (mean 11.6, 0 rank-1 winners) confirm the Economist's thesis: in seven Oscar years from 2010-2016 the Academy never crowned the year's most-referenced film. The mean annual_share captured by Best Picture winners falls from 9.4% in the 1970s to 1.5% in the 2010s — a 6.4x drop.

data_table.description: Per-decade aggregates for Best Picture winners (mean year_rank, percentage that ranked #1, mean annual_share)

ana_05.label: Best Picture winners ranked outside the top 10 of their year
ana_05.content: 22 of 89 Best Picture winners (24.7%) ranked outside the top 10 most-referenced films of their own year. The list spans every era but is concentrated in the 1980s (Out of Africa, Ordinary People, Amadeus, Gandhi all rank 16-20) and the 2010s (Spotlight ranked 25th in 2015, Moonlight 15th in 2016, Argo 11th in 2012). Cavalcade (1933, year-rank 37) and The Last Emperor (1987, year-rank 36) are historic outliers — films the Academy crowned that vanished from cultural memory almost entirely.

ana_06.label: Year-rank-1 films never nominated for Best Picture
ana_06.content: 52 of 89 year-rank-1 films (58.4%) — meaning the most-referenced film of that year — were not even nominated for Best Picture. The list reads like a syllabus of pop-cinema canon: Empire Strikes Back, Psycho, The Terminator, 2001: A Space Odyssey, Back to the Future, Return of the Jedi, Jurassic Park, The Matrix, King Kong, Frankenstein, Snow White, Die Hard, Godzilla, Halloween, Batman, The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, Aliens, The Good the Bad and the Ugly, Twilight, Bambi, RoboCop, Pinocchio, Toy Story, Vertigo, Reservoir Dogs, Singin' in the Rain, Spider-Man, The Birds, Cinderella, Star Wars VII. The Academy systematically passed over the era-defining genre films.

ana_07.label: Best Picture winners' annual_share over time
ana_07.content: Year-by-year, the share of total annual references captured by the Best Picture winner has fallen sharply. Casablanca (1943) captured 48.7% of its year's references; The Wizard of Oz year saw Gone with the Wind, the winner, take 17.7%. By contrast, the most recent winners hover near 1-2%: Spotlight 0.78%, Moonlight 1.08%, The Hurt Locker 1.81%, Birdman 1.80%, The Artist 1.53%. The Godfather (1972, 33.7%) is the modern peak. Titanic (1997, 17.2%) is the most recent winner above 10%.

ana_08.label: Median count: winners vs nominees vs unrecognized films, by decade
ana_08.content: Median connection counts dropped sharply from the 1970s peak (winners 257.5, nominees 78) to the 2010s (winners 76, nominees 41.5). Some of this is mechanical (recency problem — newer films have had less time to accrue references). But the decline is steeper for winners than for the most-referenced films overall, indicating that the Academy is choosing films further from the cultural-influence peak. The 1980s show a sharp dip in winner counts (median 129) — a decade now widely considered a low point for the Academy's choices.

ana_09.label: Concentration of references — share of #1 film, by decade
ana_09.content: The most-referenced film of each year used to dominate. In the 1970s the year-#1 captured 22.6% of all references on average. In the 2000s this fell to 7.2%, and in the 2010s to just 5.7% — a 4x drop. This is partly a function of the long tail of TV references and remake-saturation, but the underlying point is that any single film, including the Best Picture winner, has less cultural gravity in the streaming era than in the studio era. The maximum single-year share is Star Wars at 55.2% (1977); the 2010s peak is just 9.0%.

data_table.description: Annual_share of the year-#1 film, mean/median/max by decade

ana_10.label: The most-referenced film of every year (1928-2016)
ana_10.content: Year by year, the most-referenced film is rarely the Best Picture winner. Out of the years where a Best Picture was awarded, only 14 of 89 winners (15.7%) were also the year-#1. In the 1980s, the year-#1 was non-nominated five years running (Empire Strikes Back, Raiders of the Lost Ark in 1981, E.T., Return of the Jedi, The Terminator). In the 1990s and 2000s, year-#1 includes Pulp Fiction, Goodfellas, Reservoir Dogs, The Matrix, Spider-Man and Saw — none won. The list is a counter-history of Hollywood as remembered by audiences, not as honored by the Academy.

ana_12.label: Percentage of Best Picture winners ranked #1 in their year, by decade
ana_12.content: The decade-by-decade hit rate for the Academy choosing the year-#1 film tells a stark story. The 1960s and 1970s peaked at 30%. In the 1980s and 2010s, the rate falls to zero — not a single Best Picture winner was the most-referenced film of its year. Overall only 15.7% of all 89 winners were #1; the Academy is right on this metric less than one year in six.

data_table.description: Percentage of Best Picture winners that were the year-#1 most-referenced film, by decade

ana_16.label: Biggest snubs: year-#1 vs the actual Best Picture winner
ana_16.content: The most extreme mismatches are striking. In 1933 King Kong got 1,053 references and Cavalcade — the actual Best Picture winner — got 8: a count_ratio of 131. In 1931 Frankenstein had 72x more references than Cimarron. Snow White had 60x The Life of Emile Zola in 1937. In the modern era, Empire Strikes Back outpaced Ordinary People 18.6x (1980), Psycho beat The Apartment 16x (1960), and Star Wars: The Force Awakens dwarfed Spotlight 11.5x (2015). These aren't quirks — they are systematic gaps where the most-referenced film of the year was not even nominated.

caveats.content: Recency problem: counts are not comparable across years because older films have had more decades to accumulate references. Year-rank and annual_share within years are the fair comparison.
Crowdsourced data is noisy. Some 'references' are loose — actor cameos, talk-show appearances. Non-Western cinema is under-represented.
Dataset frozen at end of 2017. Late-2017 releases (notably Best Picture winner The Shape of Water) are missing or under-counted, which is why the analysis caps at 2016 releases.
Reference counts capture cultural propagation through pastiche, not artistic quality. Manos: The Hands of Fate has many references because it is famously bad.
